newsitem.title: GREECE: Guerrillas shoot dead Greek shipowner Peratikos.
newsitem.headline: Guerrillas shoot dead Greek shipowner Peratikos.

text.p: Three suspected urban guerrillas shot dead Greek shipowner Constantine Peratikos on Wednesday as he left his office and they fled in a hijacked taxi.
Police said Peratikos, 42, was ambushed in Piraeus, Greece's main port near Athens, as he was heading for a garage to get his car at about 5 p.m. (1500 GMT).
"We believe it is the work of a terrorist group, but until the ballistic tests are in we can't tell which one," a senior police officer told Reuters.
Both the November 17 and May 1 leftist groups have staged similar shooting attacks in the past.
November 17 has killed 21 Greeks and foreigners -- including the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency station chief and the U.S. military attache -- since emerging in December 1975.
But it has been dormant since a bungled rocket attack on the U.S. embassy in January 1996.
Police found .45 calibre shells at the site of the shooting. November 17 uses a trademark .45 calibre pistol to sign many of its attacks but is also versed in remote controlled bombs and rockets.
"This was the first indication that this could be a terrorist attack," police chief Athanassios Vassilopoulos told reporters at the scene.
November 17's last fatal attack was against Turkish embassy Counsellor Omer Haluk Sipahioglu, who was shot by a three-man hit squad outside his home in June 1994.
The group made its debut with a similar attack with a .45 calibre semi-automatic pistol, killing CIA station chief Richard Welch. None of its members has ever been arrested.
"It is an extremely sad event. I express my sorrow and am awaiting a detailed report from the Public Order ministry," Prime Minister Costas Simitis told reporters.
The gunmen nearly botched their escape when the van they planned to use failed to start, police said. So they hijacked a taxi passing by and sped away.
"I saw two of them as they were leaving. They had big guns. They seemed cool, as if they were well-trained," a shopowner told Greek television.
Hospital officials said Peratikos was shot seven times and died before reaching Piraeus' Tzanio hospital.
The Peratikos Group, owned by one of Greece's major shipping families, bought the troubled Elefsis Shipyards in the early 1990s. But the shipyards have since reverted to state hands.
The Peratikos family own the Piraeus-based Aran Shipping and Trading company and the London-based Pegasus Ocean Services.
